steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Antigone, a method for tuning hyperparameters of fair classifiers when sensitive attributes aren't available in either the training or the validation data. Cover the motivation, how the method works, the main results and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Bias in deep networks and fair ML
- Sensitive attributes are often unavailable
- Fair training without SA and the hyperparameter tuning problem
- Antigone: idea, pseudo-sensitive attributes, EDM
- CelebA example
- Evaluation and results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Bias in deep networks and fair ML
- DNNs succeed on real tasks but show unintended biases toward subgroups (disadvantaged groups; spurious correlations, simplicity bias)
- seminal example: commercial face recognition less accurate on darker-skinned women
- body of work on fair ML accounting for per-group performance

Sensitive attributes are often unavailable
- usual assumption: attributes like gender, race available on training + validation data -> call them sensitive attributes (SA)
- recent work: many real settings without SA
- data subjects abstain (privacy, evading future discrimination)
- discriminating attribute only known post-deployment
- fair NLP models trained on western data discriminate on last names in India
- Nikon face detection: Asian faces flagged as blinking, found retrospectively
- by then harm already done

Fair training without SA and the hyperparameter tuning problem
- recent methods train fair classifiers without SA on training set
- step 1: find advantaged / disadvantaged groups (high / low accuracy); step 2: training strategies to boost disadvantaged groups
- very sensitive to hyperparameters; can be worse than ERM without proper tuning
- so most assume SA on validation data (exceptions: GEORGE, ARL)
- but SA may be missing on validation data for the same reasons

Antigone: idea, pseudo-sensitive attributes, EDM
- Antigone: principled hyperparameter tuning for fairness, no SA on training or validation data
- enables tuning JTT, AFR (which assume ground-truth SA on validation); improves GEORGE, ARL when replacing their own tuning
- metrics: demographic parity, equal opportunity, worst sub-group accuracy
- baseline ERM trained on target labels (known, different from SA)
- advantaged groups over-represented in correctly classified set, disadvantaged in incorrectly classified set
- correct / incorrect validation data = proxies -> pseudo-sensitive attributes (PSA)
- PSA noisy; can they still be used? under mutually corrupted (MC) noise model, fairness on PSA proportional to ground-truth fairness -> usable for comparing models
- new problem: tune ERM hyperparameters to maximize PSA accuracy, but no ground-truth SA
- under MC: minimizing noise = maximizing Euclidean distance between mean (EDM) images of correct vs incorrect sets
- EDM measurable -> train family of ERM models, pick largest EDM on validation; PSAs then tune JTT, AFR, GEORGE, ARL

CelebA example
- Figure 1, CelebA: target = hair color, unknown SA = gender
- ERM discriminates against blond men
- correct set (blond) 4\% blond men vs incorrect set 65\%
- mean images: correct set more female features, incorrect set more male features
- Antigone picks ERM model with largest distance between mean images

Evaluation and results
- Antigone with JTT, AFR, GEORGE, ARL; binary SA; demographic parity, equal opportunity, worst subgroup accuracy; CelebA, Waterbirds, Adult
- (1) more accurate PSA than GEORGE's unsupervised clustering (Table 1)
- (2) with JTT (AFR) close to fairness of tuning with ground-truth SA (Table 2, Table 5)
- (3) improves GEORGE and ARL vs their own tuning (Table 3, Table 4)
- worst-group accuracy +4.2% CelebA, +8.6% Waterbirds for GEORGE; up to +11.6% Adult for ARL
- ablation / sensitivity: EDM vs alternatives (Table 1); gap between ideal MC assumptions and practice (Appendix Table 13)

Contributions
- Antigone (subsection 2.2) for overlooked problem of hyperparameter tuning for fair classification with no SA on training or validation data; PSA from correct / incorrect ERM examples
- unsupervised tuning of Antigone's own (ERM) hyperparameters by maximizing EDM; theory under MC: max EDM minimizes PSA noise in idealized setting (subsection 2.3); small gap in practice
- experiments: boosts fairness for JTT, AFR, GEORGE, ARL (section 3), beats their own tuning; more accurate PSA than GEORGE clustering (section 4)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
State-of-the-art deep neural networks have been successful on a range of real-world tasks, but prior work has found that they have unintended biases towards specific subgroups. This can be towards disadvantaged subgroups, or it can be because they tend to learn spurious correlations and have a simplicity bias, and this especially harms disadvantaged groups. For example, one seminal study showed that commercial face recognition systems had lower accuracy on darker-skinned women than on other groups. There is a body of work that tries to design fair machine learning algorithms which take into account how the model performs on each group.

Usually prior work assumes that the attributes we want to train fair models on, e.g. gender and race, are available in the training and validation data. We call these sensitive attributes (SA). But recent work has pointed out that there are many real-world settings where SA may not be available. For example, data subjects may not want to provide sensitive information, for privacy reasons or to avoid future discrimination. Also, the attributes the model discriminates on might not be known or available during training, and might only be found after deployment. For example, recent work shows that fair NLP models that were trained on western datasets discriminate based on last names when they are re-contextualized to geo-cultural settings like India. In a similar way, there are reports that Nikon's face detection models repeatedly identify Asian faces as blinking, and this bias was only identified retrospectively. By then, at least some harm has already been done.

So recent work has tried to train fair classifiers without SA on the training set. Basically these methods first find advantaged and disadvantaged groups in the training dataset, meaning subgroups with high and low accuracy. Then they use different training strategies to improve performance on the disadvantaged groups. The problem is that these methods are very sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, and without proper hyperparameter tuning they can actually hurt fairness compared to baseline empirical risk minimization (ERM). So, except for GEORGE and ARL, prior work has assumed that SA are available on the validation data. But in practical settings SA may not be available on validation data either, for the same reasons they are not available on training data.

In this paper we propose Antigone, a principled approach for hyperparameter tuning for fairness without access to SA on training and validation data. With Antigone, methods like JTT and AFR, which currently assume ground-truth SAs on validation data, can be tuned effectively, and it also improves fairness when it replaces GEORGE's and ARL's own hyperparameter tuning methods. Antigone works for different fairness metrics, including demographic parity, equal opportunity and worst sub-group accuracy.

Antigone starts with a baseline ERM model that is trained to predict target labels (these target labels are known and they are different from SAs). The subgroups that the baseline ERM model advantages will be over-represented in the set of correctly classified inputs, and in the same way the disadvantaged subgroups will be over-represented in the set of incorrectly classified inputs. So Antigone uses the correctly and incorrectly classified validation data of the ERM model as proxies for advantaged and disadvantaged subgroups. We call these pseudo-sensitive attributes (PSA). The PSA labels are noisy, because some inputs from the advantaged subgroups will be incorrectly classified and the other way around. Can they still be used for hyperparameter tuning? Prior work shows that under some theoretical assumptions on label noise, called the mutually corrupted (MC) noise model, fairness measured on PSA is proportional to ground-truth fairness. This means PSA labels on validation data can still be used to compare different models for fairness, and so also for hyperparameter tuning.

But this creates a new problem, which is how to tune the hyperparameters of the ERM model itself so that the accuracy of our PSA is maximized (or the noise is minimized). We can't measure PSA accuracy or noise directly, because we don't have any ground-truth SA labels. We show formally that under the MC noise model, minimizing noise is the same as maximizing the Euclidean distance between the mean (EDM) images in the correct and incorrect classes. The EDM can be measured directly, so we train a family of ERM models with different hyper-parameters and we pick the one with the largest EDM on the validation dataset. Then the PSAs we get are used to tune hyperparameters for fairness schemes like JTT, AFR, GEORGE and ARL.

CelebA example
- Figure 1, CelebA: target = hair color, unknown SA = gender
- ERM discriminates against blond men
- correct set (blond) 4\% blond men vs incorrect set 65\%
- mean images: correct set more female features, incorrect set more male features
- Antigone picks ERM model with largest distance between mean images

Evaluation and results
- Antigone with JTT, AFR, GEORGE, ARL; binary SA; demographic parity, equal opportunity, worst subgroup accuracy; CelebA, Waterbirds, Adult
- (1) more accurate PSA than GEORGE's unsupervised clustering (Table 1)
- (2) with JTT (AFR) close to fairness of tuning with ground-truth SA (Table 2, Table 5)
- (3) improves GEORGE and ARL vs their own tuning (Table 3, Table 4)
- worst-group accuracy +4.2% CelebA, +8.6% Waterbirds for GEORGE; up to +11.6% Adult for ARL
- ablation / sensitivity: EDM vs alternatives (Table 1); gap between ideal MC assumptions and practice (Appendix Table 13)

Contributions
- Antigone (subsection 2.2) for overlooked problem of hyperparameter tuning for fair classification with no SA on training or validation data; PSA from correct / incorrect ERM examples
- unsupervised tuning of Antigone's own (ERM) hyperparameters by maximizing EDM; theory under MC: max EDM minimizes PSA noise in idealized setting (subsection 2.3); small gap in practice
- experiments: boosts fairness for JTT, AFR, GEORGE, ARL (section 3), beats their own tuning; more accurate PSA than GEORGE clustering (section 4)

But in practical settings SA may not be available on validation data either, for the same reasons they are not available on training data.

Antigone works for different fairness metrics, including demographic parity, equal opportunity and worst sub-group accuracy.

The PSA labels are noisy, because some inputs from the advantaged subgroups will be incorrectly classified and the other way around. Can they still be used for hyperparameter tuning? Prior work shows that under some theoretical assumptions on label noise, called the mutually corrupted (MC) noise model, fairness measured on PSA is proportional to ground-truth fairness. The EDM can be measured directly, so we train a family of ERM models with different hyper-parameters and we pick the one with the largest EDM on the validation dataset. Then the PSAs we get are used to tune hyperparameters for fairness schemes like JTT, AFR, GEORGE and ARL.

As an example, look at Figure 1 on the CelebA dataset. Here the target label is hair color and the SA, which is unknown, is gender. The baseline ERM model discriminates against blond men. In the correct set for the ground-truth blond class there are only 4\% blond men, while in the incorrect set there are 65\% blond men. The mean images for the two classes show this too: the correct set for the ground-truth blond individuals has more female features and the incorrect set has more male features. Like we said above, Antigone picks the ERM model with the largest distance between these mean images, to maximize PSA label accuracy.

We evaluate Antigone together with the state-of-art methods JTT, AFR, GEORGE and ARL, on binary SA, with demographic parity, equal opportunity and worst subgroup accuracy as fairness metrics, on the CelebA, Waterbirds and Adult datasets. We find empirically that: (1) Antigone gives more accurate PSA labels on validation data than GEORGE's unsupervised clustering approach (Table 1); (2) when used with JTT (AFR), Antigone almost matches the fairness of JTT (AFR) tuned with ground-truth SA, as shown in Table 2 (Table 5); and (3) it improves the fairness of both GEORGE and ARL when Antigone's PSA labels are used in place of their own hyperparameter tuning methods (Table 3, Table 4). In particular, for GEORGE the worst-group accuracy goes up by 4.2% on CelebA and by 8.6% on Waterbirds, and for ARL it goes up by up to 11.6% on the Adult dataset.

Ablation and sensitivity studies show that Antigone's EDM metric is effective compared to alternatives (Table 1), and they also shed light on discrepancies between the ideal MC assumptions and how it is used in practice (Appendix Table 13). Overall, our key contributions are:

- We propose Antigone (subsection 2.2), a new method for hyperparameter tuning for fair classification when sensitive attributes are not available on both training and validation data, which is a problem that is often overlooked. Antigone generates PSA labels on validation data by using the correctly and incorrectly classified examples of an ERM model as proxies for advantaged and disadvantaged subgroups.

- We propose an unsupervised way to tune the hyperparameters of Antigone itself (that is, of its ERM model) by maximizing the Euclidean distance between the mean (EDM) images of the correctly and incorrectly classified sets. We justify this theoretically under the MC noise model, and prove that maximizing EDM minimizes PSA label noise in an idealized setting (subsection 2.3). Empirically, the gap between our practical implementation and the idealized MC noise model is small.

- In experiments, hyperparameter tuning based on Antigone boosts fairness for the state-of-art methods JTT, AFR, GEORGE and ARL (section 3), and even does better than their own hyperparameter tuning techniques. Antigone also gives more accurate PSA labels than GEORGE's unsupervised clustering approach (section 4).

steps.text:
Despite their success on a range of real-world tasks, prior work [1,2,3] has shown that state-of-the-art deep neural networks exhibit unintended biases towards specific subgroups, for instance towards disadvantaged subgroups or because of tendency to learn spurious correlations and simplicity bias, especially harming disadvantaged groups. For instance, seminal work by [4] showed that commercial face recognition systems had lower accuracy on darker-skinned women than other groups. A body of work has tried to design fair machine learning algorithms that account for a model’s performance on a per-group basis [5,6,7].

Prior work typically assumes that attributes, e.g. gender and race, on which we seek to train fair models are available on training and validation data [8,5]. We will refer to these as sensitive attributes (SA). However, recent work [9,10] has highlighted many real-world settings in which SA may not be available. For example, data subjects may not provide sensitive information for privacy reasons or to evade future discrimination [11]. Attributes on which the model discriminates might not be known or available during training and only identified post-deployment [12,13,14]. For instance, recent work shows that fair NLP models trained on western datasets discriminate based on last names when re-contextualized to geo-cultural settings like India [15]. Similarly, reports suggest that Nikon’s face detection models repeatedly identify Asian faces as blinking, a bias that was only identified retrospectively [16]. By this point, at least some harm has already been incurred.

Recent work has therefore sought to train fair classifiers without SA on the training set [6,17,18,3]. These methods first identify advantaged and disadvantaged groups within the training dataset; i.e., subgroups with high and low accuracy, respectively. Then, they deploy various training strategies to boost performance on disadvantaged groups. However, these methods are highly sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, and can actually hurt fairness compared to baseline empirical risk minimization (ERM) without proper hyperparameter tuning [6]. Hence, with the exception of GEORGE [7] and ARL [19], prior work has assumed access to SA on the validation data. However, in practical settings, SA may not be available for the same reasons they are unavailable on training data.

In this paper, we propose Antigone, a principled approach that enables hyperparameter tuning for fairness without access to SA on training and validation data. Antigone enables effective hyperparameter tuning of methods like JTT [6], AFR [20] (that currently assume ground-truth SAs on validation data) and improves fairness when GEORGE’s and ARL’s own hyperparameter tuning methods are replaced with Antigone. Antigone works for fairness metrics including demographic parity, equal opportunity and worst sub-group accuracy.

Antigone starts with a baseline ERM model trained to predict target labels (note these target labels are known and different from SAs). Subgroups advantaged by the baseline ERM model will be over-represented in the set of correctly classified inputs; similarly, disadvantaged subgroups are over-represented in the set of incorrectly classified inputs. Hence, Antigone uses the ERM model’s correctly and incorrectly classified validation data as proxies for advantaged and disadvantaged subgroups, respectively. We refer to these as pseudo-sensitive attributes (PSA). Note that PSA labels are noisy; some inputs from the advantaged subgroups will be incorrectly classified, and vice-versa. Can they still be used for hyperparameter tuning? Prior work shows that under certain theoretical assumptions on label noise, called the mutually corrupted (MC) noise model, fairness measured on PSA is proportional to ground-truth fairness [21]. Thus, PSA labels on validation data can still be used to compare different models for fairness, and consequently for hyperparameter tuning.

However, this sets up a new problem: how do we tune the hyperparameters of the ERM model itself to maximize the accuracy (or minimize the noise) of our PSA? We cannot directly measure PSA accuracy or noise since we do not have any ground-truth SA labels. Here, we show formally that under the MC noise model, minimizing noise is equivalent to maximizing the Euclidean distance between the mean (EDM) images in the correct and incorrect classes. Since EDM can be measured directly, we train a family of ERM models with different hyper-parameters and pick the model with the largest EDM on the validation dataset. The PSAs obtained are then used to tune hyperparameters for fairness schemes like JTT, AFR, GEORGE and ARL.

To give some intuition, consider the example in Figure 1 on the CelebA dataset. The target label is hair color, and the (unknown) SA is gender. The baseline ERM model discriminates against blond men. The correct set for the ground-truth blond class has only 4\% blond men while the incorrect set has 65\% blond men. This is also reflected in the mean images for these two classes: the correct set for the ground-truth blond individuals has more female features while the incorrect set has more male features. As noted above, Antigone picks an ERM model with the largest distance between these mean images so as to maximize PSA label accuracy.

We evaluate Antigone in conjunction with three state-of-art methods, JTT [6], AFR [20], GEORGE [7] and ARL [19], on binary SA using demographic parity, equal opportunity, and worst subgroup accuracy as fairness metrics across the CelebA, Waterbirds and Adult datasets. We find empirically that: (1) Antigone produces more accurate PSA labels on validation data compared to GEORGE’s unsupervised clustering approach (Table 1); (2) used with JTT (AFR), Antigone comes close to matching the fairness of JTT (AFR) tuned with ground-truth SA as shown in Table 2 (Table 5); and (3) improves the fairness of both GEORGE and ARL when Antigone’s PSA labels are used instead of their own hyperparameter tuning methods (Table 3, Table 4). In particular, the worst-group accuracy increases by 4.2% and 8.6% on the CelebA and Waterbirds datasets for GEORGE, respectively, and by up to 11.6% on the Adult dataset for ARL.

Ablation and sensitivity studies demonstrate the effectiveness of Antigone’s EDM metric versus alternatives (Table 1) and shed light on discrepancies between the ideal MC assumptions and its use in practice (Appendix Table 13). Overall, our key contributions are:

- • We propose Antigone (subsection 2.2), a new method for the often overlooked problem of hyperparameter tuning for fair classification in setting where sensitive attributes are unavailable on both training and validation data. Antigone generates PSA labels on validation data using the correctly and incorrectly classified examples of an ERM model as proxies for advantaged and disadvantaged subgroups.

- • We propose an unsupervised approach to tune Antigone’s own hyperparameters (specifically, those of its ERM model) by maximizing the Euclidean distance between the mean (EDM) images of the correctly and incorrectly classified sets. We theoretically justify this choice under the MC noise model, proving that maximizing EDM minimizes PSA label noise in an idealized setting (subsection 2.3). Empirically, we show that the gap between our practical implementation and the idealized MC noise model is small.

- • Experimentally, we find that Antigone based hyperparameter tuning boosts fairness for three state-of-art methods, JTT, AFR, GEORGE and ARL (section 3), even surpassing their own hyperparameter tuning techniques. Antigone also generates more accurate PSA labels compared to GEORGE’s unsupervised clustering approach (section 4).
